analysis.one_liner: Raises fuel-economy standards for cars and trucks while funding U.S. plant retooling for advanced vehicles.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill with 178 cosponsors to raise automobile fuel-economy standards never got a vote, dying in a House Energy and Commerce subcommittee.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have directed the Transportation Department to keep raising average fuel-economy standards for cars and light trucks, aiming for a combined fleet average of no more than 35 miles per gallon by model year 2022 and at least 32 thereafter. It let standards be set based on vehicle attributes, let manufacturers trade fuel-economy credits within their own fleets, and created a Treasury account, funded partly by civil penalties on rule-breakers, to pay grants for reequipping U.S. plants to build advanced-technology vehicles. It also created a tire fuel-efficiency rating system for shoppers and a public fuel-conservation education campaign. Despite 178 cosponsors split between both parties, it never left committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Drivers who would save money on gasoline as fleets became more efficient, along with everyone affected by lower tailpipe carbon emissions. Domestic automakers and their parts suppliers also benefit: they gain an alternative minimum standard that applies only to their domestically built cars, flexibility to trade credits across their own fleets, and federal grants to retool plants.

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires the Secretary of Transportation to set the maximum feasible average fuel-economy standards for passenger and non-passenger automobiles, with a projected combined average of no more than 35 mpg for model year 2022 and not less than 32 mpg after that.

It creates a Treasury account, funded by civil penalties on manufacturers that violate the standards, to make grants to automakers and component suppliers to reequip or expand U.S. facilities producing advanced-technology vehicles and components.

It directs a national tire fuel-efficiency rating and consumer information program so tire buyers can see how replacement tires affect fuel economy, and funds a public education campaign on fuel-conserving measures.
It lets manufacturers transfer fuel-economy credits within their own fleets across car categories, capped at a 1.0 mpg boost in any single model year.

analysis.who_pays: Automakers bear the cost of meeting higher standards, which can feed into vehicle prices, and taxpayers cover the public education campaign and any appropriated additions to the retooling grant account.

drawbacks.text: The bill includes a special alternative minimum standard applying only to a manufacturer's domestically built passenger cars — 27.5 mpg or 92 percent of the projected fleetwide average, whichever is greater — meaning cars built in U.S. plants could be held to a weaker standard than the rest of the fleet, shrinking the fuel savings consumers would otherwise get.

Attribute-based standards (standards sized to each vehicle's characteristics) give larger, less-efficient vehicles easier targets, a flexibility that critics of such schemes argued reduces total fuel savings compared with a flat fleetwide number.

The retooling grant program and a 10-year extension of manufacturing incentives for alternative-fuel vehicles shift taxpayer money toward manufacturers, on top of the compliance flexibility the bill gives them.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core of the bill — steadily rising fuel-economy standards — would save drivers real money at the pump and cut emissions, and the tire-labeling program is a low-cost consumer win. But the bill was written to soften the blow for domestic automakers: the domestic-fleet minimum standard and attribute-based flexibility would have delivered less savings than a straightforwardly strict standard. As a compromise it was genuinely two-sided, which is also why it drew criticism from both directions.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Energy and Air Quality subcommittee the day it was introduced, and it never got a markup or floor vote before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 28, 2007, by Rep. Baron Hill with six original cosponsors, and referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
Also on June 28, 2007, it was referred to the subcommittee on Energy and Air Quality — the last action the bill ever received.
It drew 178 cosponsors, including 114 Republicans and 64 Democrats, but the full committee never reported it out and the House never voted on it.

The bill text would have required standards pushing the combined new-vehicle fleet average to no more than 35 mpg for model year 2022 and at least 32 mpg thereafter, while carving out an alternative minimum standard for domestically manufactured passenger cars and creating a Treasury account to fund plant-retooling grants.
The 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009, with the bill still sitting in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Domestic automakers were spared a new statutory standard that included a taxpayer-funded retooling account and a credit-trading program. In practical terms consumers lost little, because separate energy legislation enacted later in 2007 raised fuel-economy standards anyway — without this bill's weaker floor for domestically built cars — so the bill's manufacturer-specific carve-outs died with it.

for.name: Rep. Baron Hill
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to raise CAFE standards and fund domestic advanced-vehicle production.

for.name: 178 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it broad bipartisan support.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over fuel-economy standards
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Energy and Air Quality subcommittee on the day of introduction and never brought it to a markup or reported it to the House during the two-and-a-half-year life of the Congress.

against.name: Rep. John Dingell
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee that held the bill in subcommittee without action; he was widely known during this period as the House's leading defender of the auto industry's position on fuel-economy rules.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was heavily bipartisan — 114 Republicans and 64 Democrats — yet the bill died without action in a committee controlled by Democrats, so the barrier was jurisdiction and committee leadership rather than a partisan floor vote.

industries.note: The bill would have raised the standards automakers must meet, but it also locked in their advantages: a separate minimum standard for domestically built cars, credit trading within their own fleets, and a Treasury account paying grants to retool U.S. plants. The industry would have gained a permanent federal funding channel for advanced-vehicle production even while accepting tighter rules.

The alternative minimum standard applies only to domestically manufactured passenger cars, so brands whose U.S. sales are largely imported would have faced relatively tougher compliance than manufacturers with big domestic fleets.
Higher fuel economy means less gasoline sold per mile driven; the industry's loss in this bill runs opposite to drivers' savings at the pump.

They would have to run standardized tests and label replacement tires for fuel efficiency, with civil penalties up to $50,000 per violation, in exchange for a rating system that helps buyers compare products.
